title: OpenAI’s Browser Could Be Hijacked to Spam Your WhatsApp Contacts
gist: Security firm Zenity found around 20 flaws across AI-enabled browsers from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Microsoft and Perplexity, including a worm-style attack on OpenAI's Atlas browser (being deprecated August 9) that used Hebrew-language prompt injection to hijack a user's WhatsApp Web session and mass-message every contact, plus a bypass that let attackers add items to a logged-in Amazon cart by directly asking Amazon's own Rufus AI assistant to complete the purchase.

themes.theme: Systemic weakness across AI browsers, not just one product

insights.claim: Security firm Zenity found around 20 flaws across leading AI-enabled web browsers and browser extensions, including products from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Perplexity, which collectively allowed researchers to access local machines, grab files, take over a password manager, and leak someone's entire browsing history.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A ~20-flaw count spanning five major AI browser vendors indicates the security gaps are structural to the agentic-browsing category itself, not isolated to one company's implementation — a sector-wide risk relevant to any enterprise adopting AI browser agents.

insights.claim: Zenity cofounder and CTO Michael Bargury says AI browser vendors have 'nerfed the security control of browsers' to the point that researchers are now seeing the kinds of attacks common on browsers 20 years ago, before modern browser security protections were developed.
insights.speaker: Michael Bargury (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: A direct characterization from a security researcher that AI browser agents have regressed browser security by two decades is a strong warning signal for enterprises considering deployment of AI browsing agents on sensitive accounts.
insights.quote: They have nerfed the security control of browsers—we are now back to seeing the kinds of attacks that you saw on browsers 20 years ago.
insights.locator: says Michael Bargury, cofounder and CTO of Zenity

insights.claim: Of all the AI browser tools probed, OpenAI's Atlas — which the company is shutting down the following week — had the most protections and security boundaries in place among those tested, though researchers were still able to bypass them; other browsing tools tested were described as much easier to hack.
insights.speaker: Michael Bargury (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Even the best-defended product in the category (Atlas) was still bypassable, implying the weaker competing AI browsers likely present significantly higher real-world exploitation risk for their users right now.

insights.claim: The article notes that long-standing web security practices such as the same-origin policy — which stops websites from interacting with each other — can be rendered 'effectively useless' once an AI agent is exposed to untrusted web data and processes it as instructions.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Same-origin policy is a foundational web security control; if AI agents can systematically bypass it via prompt injection, this represents a category-level failure of decades-old browser security architecture, not a patchable bug.
insights.locator: long-standing web security practices, such as same-origin policy

themes.theme: The WhatsApp worm and Amazon purchase bypass

insights.claim: Zenity researchers got Atlas to sign up for a fake newsletter whose page contained Hebrew-language instructions telling the AI to navigate to the user's signed-in WhatsApp Web account and send the same message to every contact; the technique bypassed OpenAI's safeguards by using a legitimate-looking sign-up page, writing instructions in Hebrew to evade English-language security tools, and falsely claiming the system was a sandboxed WhatsApp environment with fake contacts.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A working proof-of-concept turns an AI browser agent into a self-propagating messaging worm across a user's real contact network — the specific evasion techniques (non-English language, fake-legitimacy framing, false sandbox claims) are a documented playbook other attackers could replicate against similar agentic browsers.

insights.claim: Bargury describes the attack as self-propagating: Atlas would go through each and every contact and send the same newsletter-signup instructions, meaning each infected contact's own AI agent (if compromised similarly) could further spread the attack to their contacts.
insights.speaker: Michael Bargury (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: The worm-like propagation mechanic through personal contact networks is a materially more dangerous threat model than a single-account compromise, since it can cascade across a social graph without further attacker action.
insights.quote: What it'll do is go through each and every one of the contacts and send the instructions to join this newsletter as well—so this is a worm. So you are now infecting the rest of your friends and family.
insights.locator: What it'll do is go through each and every one

insights.claim: The researchers describe the underlying mechanism as 'intent collision,' where the AI agent merges a user's legitimate instructions with malicious instructions embedded in web content to complete a hacker's goal rather than the user's actual intent.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Names a specific, generalizable failure mode ('intent collision') for agentic AI systems that blend trusted user commands with untrusted web content — a useful conceptual model for evaluating any AI agent's security architecture going forward.
insights.locator: The researchers say the attack is an example

insights.claim: Using the same fake-newsletter technique, researchers got Atlas to add a shipping address to a logged-in Amazon account and place a tablet in the shopping cart, but could not find a way to bypass OpenAI's safeguards to force Atlas itself to complete the purchase; instead, they got Atlas to ask Amazon's own Rufus AI shopping assistant to make the purchase, and Rufus was not hijacked or injected but simply complied because it believed it was being asked by the legitimate customer.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: This reveals a distinct bypass technique — routing a blocked action through a second, unhijacked AI assistant that trusts the first agent's request at face value — showing that per-agent safety controls can be defeated by exploiting trust between cooperating AI systems, a risk relevant to any multi-agent commerce integration.
insights.quote: Rufus was not hijacked or injected, it was just asked, by what it took to be the customer, and it complied.
insights.locator: In the end, they say, they got Atlas to ask Amazon's Rufus

insights.claim: Zenity reported its findings to OpenAI in January; OpenAI says it deployed an update earlier this year to address the issue and strengthen protections in Atlas, which is being deprecated on August 9, and says these protections extend to the browser capabilities in the new ChatGPT app.
insights.speaker: OpenAI spokesperson (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: OpenAI is discontinuing Atlas within days of this disclosure while porting the same browser capabilities (and claimed protections) into the ChatGPT app, meaning the underlying security model — not just the Atlas product — is what actually matters going forward for OpenAI's browsing features.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, we deployed an update

insights.claim: OpenAI's own security lead has previously described prompt-injection attacks as an 'unsolved security problem,' and the article notes the attacks are complex — real-world criminal hackers generally have far easier methods available, like direct phishing or using stolen login credentials, rather than crafting agentic-AI prompt-injection exploits.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Provides useful risk calibration: while the vulnerability class is real and unsolved, current criminal incentives still favor simpler attack methods, suggesting near-term real-world exploitation volume may lag the theoretical severity of the flaw class.
insights.locator: The attacks are, as OpenAI's security boss said last year

insights.claim: Bargury argues that AI system designers should use 'deterministic' or hard security barriers rather than relying on the judgments or classifications made by AI systems themselves, since AI-based judgment can nearly always be fooled, and urges careful limits on what level of access and agency AI agents are given within browsers.
insights.speaker: Michael Bargury (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable security design principle — hard-coded deterministic barriers over AI-judgment-based safety — that enterprise security teams evaluating or deploying AI browser agents should require from vendors.
insights.quote: You are putting yourself in a situation where the browser can completely get hijacked and your accounts can get compromised, your data can leak.
insights.locator: the Zenity researchers say that when designing AI systems
